stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Volunteer mapping platforms let anyone add roads and buildings to a shared digital map. When geographer Lina Okafor compared one such map of Nairobi with the official city map, she found that new roads appeared on the volunteer map within weeks, while the official map took years to show them. Volunteer maps, she concluded, can track urban change remarkably quickly.

Text 2
Okafor's findings certainly show what volunteer mapping does well. But volunteers tend to map the places where they live and work. In thinly populated rural districts, where few contributors are active, volunteer maps often remain sparse and outdated.
choices: Volunteer maps can show some new roads sooner than official maps do.
Volunteer maps are as complete in rural areas as they are in cities.
Volunteer maps are too unreliable to be useful in any setting.
Official maps of Nairobi are drawn mostly by volunteer contributors.
explanation: Text 2 opens by crediting Okafor's findings ('certainly show what volunteer mapping does well') before turning on 'But' to add a limit about rural areas. What both authors accept is the conceded point: in places like Nairobi, volunteer maps record new roads faster than official maps.

B.why: You ignored the caveat after 'But'. Text 2 says rural volunteer maps stay sparse and outdated, so its author would reject this.

C.why: You read 'But' as full disagreement. Text 2 explicitly grants that volunteer mapping does some things well, so it does not throw volunteer maps out.

D.why: Text 1 sets the official map against the volunteer map. Neither text says volunteers draw the official map.

subtype_name: Yes-but: Text 2 accepts Text 1 and adds a limit

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Planting a cover crop such as winter rye after harvest keeps soil anchored through the off-season. In a four-year trial in Iowa, agronomist Dale Brennan found that fields planted with rye lost about half as much topsoil to erosion as fields left bare. Brennan therefore recommends cover crops as a reliable way to protect farmland.

Text 2
Brennan's erosion results deserve attention. Still, rye draws water from the soil as it grows. In semiarid regions, where spring moisture is scarce, a cover crop can leave too little water for the cash crop that follows, lowering yields.
choices: Cover crops are equally beneficial in dry and wet regions.
Cover crops do little to protect soil from erosion.
Cover crops like rye can reduce topsoil loss from erosion.
Cover crops are valued mainly as feed for livestock.
explanation: Text 2 concedes that Brennan's erosion results 'deserve attention', then pivots on 'Still' to add a cost in dry regions. The point both authors share is the one Text 2 grants: rye and similar cover crops cut erosion.

A.why: You picked pure agreement and skipped the caveat. Text 2 says cover crops can lower yields in semiarid regions, so it would not call them equally beneficial everywhere.

B.why: You read 'Still' as a rejection of Text 1. Text 2 accepts the erosion findings and disputes only how well cover crops work in dry places.

D.why: Neither text mentions livestock feed. Both are about erosion and soil moisture.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Online projects invite volunteers to sort telescope images of galaxies by shape: spiral, elliptical, or irregular. When astronomers checked thousands of these volunteer labels against classifications made by professionals, the two agreed in over 90 percent of cases. Volunteers, the team concluded, are reliable classifiers of galaxy shapes.

Text 2
Such checks have shown that volunteers sort bright, nearby galaxies well. But most of the images checked showed exactly those galaxies. For faint, distant galaxies, whose features are blurred, volunteer labels and expert labels diverge far more often.
choices: Volunteers classify faint galaxies as accurately as professionals do.
Volunteers can reliably sort the shapes of bright, nearby galaxies.
Volunteer galaxy labels should not be used in any research.
Professionals classify galaxies less accurately than volunteers.
explanation: Text 2 grants that the checks 'have shown that volunteers sort bright, nearby galaxies well', then turns on 'But' to narrow the claim for faint, distant galaxies. Both authors accept the narrowed claim: volunteers are reliable on bright, nearby galaxies.

A.why: You ignored the limit Text 2 adds. It says volunteer and expert labels diverge far more often for faint galaxies.

C.why: You treated 'But' as full disagreement. Text 2 credits volunteers' work on bright galaxies, so it does not reject their labels entirely.

D.why: Text 1 uses professionals as the standard that volunteers are checked against. Neither author says volunteers beat them.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Permeable pavement is made of concrete riddled with tiny pores that let rainwater drain into the ground beneath. When engineers installed it in a test parking lot in Ohio, the lot absorbed nearly all the rain from a series of heavy storms, sending little runoff into nearby sewers. The engineers concluded that permeable pavement can ease the strain on city drainage systems.

Text 2
The Ohio results are encouraging. It's important to consider, though, that the test lot was new. Over several years, sand and grit wash into the pores and clog them, and unless the pavement is regularly vacuumed, it absorbs far less water.
choices: Permeable pavement keeps absorbing rain equally well for decades.
Permeable pavement fails to reduce runoff even when newly laid.
Permeable pavement is cheaper to install than ordinary concrete.
Newly laid permeable pavement can absorb much of the rain on it.
explanation: Text 2 calls the Ohio results 'encouraging', then pivots with 'It's important to consider, though' to add a longer time frame: the pores clog over the years. Both authors accept what the new test lot showed, which is that fresh permeable pavement absorbs most of the rain that falls on it.

A.why: You picked pure agreement and missed the caveat. Text 2 says the pavement absorbs far less water after several years unless it is maintained.

B.why: You read the pivot as full disagreement. Text 2 accepts the Ohio results for a new lot and questions only how long they last.

C.why: Neither text discusses cost, so you can't attribute this view to either author.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Winter is hard on small songbirds, which must eat constantly to stay warm. In a study in Wisconsin, ornithologist Mara Lindqvist tracked banded black-capped chickadees and found that birds with access to backyard feeders were more likely to survive the winter than birds without them. Feeders, she suggests, give small birds a valuable edge in cold months.

Text 2
Lindqvist's survival data certainly offer encouraging insight. But feeders also crowd many birds into one small space. Among house finches, that crowding has helped spread an eye disease that passes easily between birds sharing a feeding surface.
choices: Feeders do more harm than good and should be removed.
Feeders can improve some small songbirds' odds of surviving winter.
Feeders pose no health risks to the birds that visit them.
Chickadees are more vulnerable to eye disease than finches are.
explanation: Text 2 begins by granting that Lindqvist's data 'certainly offer encouraging insight', then turns on 'But' to name a cost Text 1 left out: disease spreads at crowded feeders. Both authors accept the conceded point that feeders help small birds like chickadees survive winter.

A.why: You read 'But' as full disagreement. Text 2 credits the survival findings and adds a cost. It never says feeders should be removed.

C.why: You took the agreement and skipped the caveat. Text 2 says crowding at feeders has helped spread an eye disease among house finches.

D.why: Neither text compares how vulnerable the two species are. Text 2 mentions the disease only in house finches.
